title: Fit a servo horn onto its splined output shaft with the horn arm on the zero mark
instruction: Fit the white servo horn onto the servo's splined output shaft with its arm lined up on the engraved zero mark, then let go.
context: Building a robot arm means fitting a servo horn on each joint's 25-tooth output shaft. The horn seats at only 25 angles, 14.4 deg apart, so the technician lines its arm up on the engraved zero mark before pressing; pressed where it lands, the joint is off by whole teeth and every later calibration inherits it. This is the assembly step behind the arms that collect robot-learning data, and a robot able to do it can build and repair its own hardware.
setup: Station table; positions in metres, x forward from the arm bases, y to the robot's left, z up; table top at z 0.7475. (1) Hobby servo: black ABS/aluminium case 40.7 x 19.7 x 36 mm, 55 g, long axis along x, bolted to the bench (fixed); silver 11.5 mm boss 3 mm tall on the case top and a silver 25-tooth output shaft 5.9 mm across, 5 mm proud of the boss, on the case top 10 mm from its -x end, at (0.250, -0.050). A white 1.2 x 24 mm zero mark is engraved on the case top from the boss out along +x. (2) Servo horn: white nylon single-arm horn, 4 g, a 14 mm x 7 mm hub with a 6.8 mm bore and a 28 mm arm 2 mm thick, lying flat at (0.220, -0.220), arm pointing 68 deg from +x (4 deg from a spline position). Crest on crest the horn stands 1.5 mm proud of the boss; it seats (hub flush on the boss) only when its bore is within 0.8 mm of the shaft, tilt 4 deg or less, and the arm within 2.0 deg of one of the 25 positions (every 14.4 deg from the zero mark), under a press of about 3.6 N. A seated horn does not come off. Real parts: any 25T hobby servo (MG996R size) and its single-arm horn; verify the stand-off with a 1.5 mm feeler gauge and the press with a kitchen scale.
scoring: Whole-run record, every control step, cleared only by the simulator reset. Arm azimuth a is the horn arm's angle from the zero mark (top view); index k = round(a / 14.4). Gate (score 0 for the run): the horn ever seats (hub flush within 0.3 mm of the boss) at k not 0, or more than 2.0 deg from the mark. 0.25: a gripper holds the horn (pad within 4 mm, opening 30 mm or less) with its bore within 1.0 mm of the shaft, tilt 4 deg or less, resting on the crests and its arm within 3.0 deg of the mark. 0.5: the horn seated at index 0 (arm within 2.0 deg of the mark) at some time. 0.75: at the end still seated flush (gap 0.5 mm or less), tilt 2 deg or less, bore within 0.8 mm of the shaft, arm within 2.0 deg of the mark. 1.0: also the horn still (under 2 mm/s and 2 deg/s) and both grippers at least 30 mm from the horn and servo and moving under 5 mm/s for the last 1 s. Real trial: top photo with a ruler for the arm against the engraved mark (2.0 deg is 1.0 mm sideways at the arm tip); a 0.5 mm feeler gauge under the hub for flush seating; the horn seated at any other tooth, seen as the arm 14.4 deg or more off the mark, scores 0; a video frame for the hold and the 1 s release.
reset_notes: Nothing is consumed. Pull the horn off the shaft with a servo-horn puller (or a 4 mm bolt through the hub), lay it flat at (0.220, -0.220) with its arm 68 deg from +x (taped outline), and check with the 1.5 mm feeler gauge that a crest-on-crest horn stands proud again. The servo stays bolted.
fidelity: True-size servo and horn, 25 teeth at 14.4 deg. The teeth themselves are not modelled: a spring seat ring (3.6 N at 1.5 mm, held by a brake once flush) may travel only when the bore is on the shaft and the arm is within 2.0 deg of an index. The 1.5 mm crest stand-off and 3.6 N are set for the arm's pressing force, not measured on a real servo. Rigid, no wear.
